takeaways: A theodolite gives true angles only when its lines keep their relations; temporary adjustments are made at every station, permanent ones only after a failed test.
Reading both verniers removes eccentricity; the mean of both faces removes collimation, trunnion-axis and index errors, but not a tilted vertical axis.
Repetition reduces reading and graduation errors; the direction method handles many stations and checks itself by closing the horizon.
Trigonometric levelling adds D tan α to the RL of the instrument axis; for an inaccessible base two stations and a base give D.
With a vertical staff on an inclined sight, D = K s cos²θ + C cos θ; C is zero only with an anallatic lens or internal focusing.
Triangulation scales every side from the base, so the base is measured with every correction, including the reduction to mean sea level.
Control is closed, checked and adjusted before detail is hung on it; the relative precision 1 in (Σl ÷ e) is what is compared with the specification.
Weights go as 1 ÷ σ²; least squares minimises Σwv²; a residual beyond about 3σ is a mistake to remeasure.
On a circular curve, T₂ = T₁ + l and the total deflection to T₂ is Δ/2; a transition grows the curvature steadily and a vertical parabola joins two gradients.
bank_note: Most papers ask for the permanent adjustments of a theodolite, a measurement of an angle by repetition, a single plane or double plane height, a tacheometric reduction, a triangle or traverse computed to coordinates and, where curves are taught, a Rankine table. Write the formula, substitute with units, and end every calculation with a check.

bank.q: Name the fundamental lines of a transit theodolite and the relations between them in a correctly adjusted instrument. Describe the permanent adjustments in the order in which they are made, giving the test and the correction for each.
outline: Collimation test with marks B, C and D
answer: Fundamental lines: the vertical axis (about which the instrument turns), the horizontal or trunnion axis (about which the telescope tilts), the line of collimation (through the intersection of the cross-hairs and the optical centre of the objective), the axis of the plate level, and the axis of the altitude level.

Required relations: (1) the plate level axis is perpendicular to the vertical axis; (2) the vertical cross-hair lies in a plane perpendicular to the horizontal axis; (3) the line of collimation is perpendicular to the horizontal axis; (4) the horizontal axis is perpendicular to the vertical axis; (5) the altitude level axis is parallel to the line of collimation, and the vertical circle reads zero when the line of sight is horizontal.

Order: the adjustments are made in the order 1 to 5, because each test assumes the earlier relations already hold. A collimation test made with a faulty plate level, for example, would mix two errors.

Plate level adjustment. Test: level up carefully, then swing the upper plate through 180° about the vertical axis. If the bubble stays central the level is in adjustment. If it runs n divisions, the error is n/2, because swinging reverses the tilted vial. Correction: bring the bubble back halfway (n/2) with the capstan screws at one end of the vial and the other half with the foot screws; repeat until it stays central in all positions. Example: a run of 4 divisions of 20″ is an error of 40″.

Cross-hair ring adjustment. Test: sight a fine point with one end of the vertical hair and tilt the telescope with the vertical tangent screw; the point must stay on the hair. Correction: loosen two adjacent capstan screws of the diaphragm and rotate the ring until it does.

Collimation adjustment (line of sight perpendicular to the horizontal axis). Test on level ground: set up at O, sight A about 100 m away on face left, transit and mark B about 100 m beyond O; change face, sight A again, transit and mark C beside B. Each face throws the line 2c off the straight, to opposite sides, so BC = 4c × OB. Correction: move the vertical hair with the side capstan screws until it cuts D, one quarter of BC from C; repeat. Example: BC = 24 mm at 100 m gives c = 0.024 ÷ 400 = 0.00006 rad ≈ 12″, and D is 6 mm from C.

Horizontal axis adjustment (spire test). Test: set up near a tall building, sight a high point such as a spire on face left, depress the telescope and mark a point P near ground level; change face and repeat to get Q. If P and Q differ, the horizontal axis is not perpendicular to the vertical axis. Correction: sight the midpoint of PQ, raise the telescope (it will miss the spire) and raise or lower one end of the trunnion axis with the screw in the standard until the hair cuts the spire.

Vertical index and altitude level adjustment. Test: centre the altitude bubble, sight a fine point on both faces and read the vertical angles. If they differ, the index is in error by half the difference. Correction: keep the hair on the point, set the vernier to the mean angle with the clip screw, which moves the bubble off; re-centre the altitude bubble with its own capstan screws. Repeat until both faces agree.

Summary of what remains: after these adjustments small residual errors are still eliminated in practice by observing on both faces and reading both verniers; only a vertical axis that is not truly vertical cannot be eliminated by changing face, so levelling up is done with special care before steep sights.

bank.q: Describe the temporary adjustments of a theodolite. Explain how a horizontal angle is measured by the method of repetition on both faces, and state which errors this procedure eliminates or reduces.
outline: Levelling up with two and then three foot screws
Repetition steps with upper and lower clamps
Booking and computing on both faces
Errors removed: eccentricity, collimation, trunnion, graduation, reading
answer: Setting up: spread the tripod legs over the station with the head roughly level and fix the instrument. Centring: move the legs and then the shifting head until the plumb bob or optical plummet is exactly over the station mark.

Levelling up: turn the plate so that one plate level is parallel to two foot screws; turn those two screws together, thumbs moving both inward or both outward, until the bubble is central (it follows the left thumb). Turn through 90° and centre the bubble with the third screw alone. Repeat until the bubble stays central in every direction, and recheck the centring.

Focusing the eyepiece on the cross-hairs against a bright background, then the objective on the target. Removing parallax: if the cross-hair seems to move over the target when the eye moves, refocus the objective until it does not.
Repetition, face left: with the upper clamp, set vernier A to 0°00′00″. Release the lower clamp, sight the left station P, bisect it with the lower tangent screw, and read both verniers.
Release the upper clamp, turn clockwise to R and bisect with the upper tangent screw. Note the reading roughly (first repetition).

Release the lower clamp, turn back to P (the reading stays on the circle) and bisect with the lower tangent screw. Release the upper clamp, turn to R and bisect with the upper tangent screw; the circle now shows twice the angle. Repeat until three repetitions are complete and read both verniers.
Change face and repeat three repetitions on face right.

answer.text: Computation (example, angle PQR with a 20″ instrument):

answer: Final angle = ½(42°51′20″ + 42°51′40″) = 42°51′30″. The 20″ difference between faces is acceptable for this instrument.

Errors eliminated or reduced: eccentricity of verniers and circle by reading both verniers; collimation error, horizontal axis error and errors of a misplaced index by the mean of the two faces; graduation error, because the repetitions use different parts of the circle (further reduced by changing the initial setting between sets); reading error, because the least count is divided by the number of repetitions.

Not eliminated: a vertical axis that is not truly vertical (it does not reverse with the face), errors of centring and bisection, and refraction. These are kept small by careful levelling and centring, sighting the foot of a ranging rod, and observing in steady air.

bank.q: Derive the distance equation D = K s + C for a stadia tacheometer with a horizontal line of sight, and explain the meaning of K and C. Explain how the constants are found in the field and how an anallatic lens affects C.
outline: K = f ÷ i and C = f + d
Field determination from two taped distances
answer: The diaphragm carries two stadia hairs, a fixed distance i apart, above and below the central hair. Rays through the outer hairs cut a vertical staff at two points; the difference of the readings is the staff intercept s.

Let f be the focal length of the objective, u the distance from the optical centre of the objective to the staff, and v the distance from the objective to the image (the plane of the diaphragm). The image of the intercept s is the hair interval i.
By similar triangles through the optical centre, s ÷ i = u ÷ v. By the lens formula, 1/u + 1/v = 1/f.
Multiplying the lens formula by u f: f + f u/v = u, so u = f + f (u/v) = f + f (s/i) = (f/i) s + f.
The distance D from the vertical axis of the instrument to the staff is u + d, where d is the distance from the objective's optical centre to the vertical axis. So D = (f/i) s + (f + d) = K s + C.

K = f/i is the multiplying constant; the maker spaces the hairs so that K = 100. C = f + d is the additive constant, about 0.3 to 0.45 m in an external-focusing telescope, where the objective is moved out on a slide to focus.

Field determination: on level ground, tape two or more distances from the instrument, for example D₁ = 50.000 m and D₂ = 100.000 m, and read the intercepts, say s₁ = 0.496 m and s₂ = 0.996 m. Then 100.000 = 0.996K + C and 50.000 = 0.496K + C. Subtracting, 50.000 = 0.500K, so K = 100, and C = 50.000 − 49.600 = 0.400 m. With more distances, the constants are found as the best fit (least squares) and the readings are repeated.

Anallatic lens: an extra convex lens fixed between the objective and the eyepiece of an external-focusing telescope, placed so that the apex of the cone of stadia rays falls exactly at the vertical axis. Then C = 0 and D = K s directly, so the field reduction is simpler.

Internal-focusing telescopes focus by moving a concave lens inside a tube of fixed length; their additive constant is only a few centimetres and is taken as zero, so most modern tacheometers behave as anallatic.

On an inclined sight to a vertical staff the same constants are used in D = K s cos²θ + C cos θ and V = ½ K s sin 2θ + C sin θ; with the constants above, s = 1.250 m and θ = 8°12′ give D = 122.85 m and V = 17.70 m.
Check of the field values: K s + C for the 50 m staff gives 100 × 0.496 + 0.400 = 50.000 m, as taped.

bank.q: Explain the principle of triangulation. Describe the classification of triangulation systems, the figures used, the conditions for a well-conditioned triangle, and the corrections applied to a measured base line.
outline: Base, angles, sine rule; check base
Primary, secondary, tertiary with side lengths and closures
Base corrections: standard, temperature, pull, sag, slope, MSL
answer: Principle: a network of triangles is laid over the area. One side, the base, is measured very precisely, and every angle is observed. Each triangle is solved by the sine rule, a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C, so each computed side becomes the known side of the next triangle. A second measured base (check base) at the far end tests the whole chain. Coordinates of the stations follow from the sides and their bearings.

Figures: a chain of single triangles is quick but has only the angle sum of each triangle as a check; braced quadrilaterals (four stations, both diagonals observed) are the strongest and suit long narrow strips such as a highway; centred polygons (a ring of triangles about a central station) suit wide areas.

Well-conditioned triangle: no angle less than about 30° or more than 120°. The best shape is isosceles with base angles of 56°14′, which makes the error in the computed sides least for a given angle error, because the rate of change of sin A is small away from 0° and 180°. Strength of figure is a number computed from the angles of a layout to compare how much angle error grows into side error; the layout with the lower value is chosen.
Station selection: intervisible stations, well-shaped triangles, lines clear of the ground and buildings (with towers where needed), easy access, firm ground for permanent marks.

Base line corrections, applied to the measured length L: standardisation (tape length differs from nominal); temperature Ct = α (Tm − T₀) L; pull Cp = (P − P₀) L ÷ (A E); sag Cs = −w² l³ ÷ (24 P²) for each suspended span l; slope −h² ÷ (2L) or L(1 − cos θ); and reduction to mean sea level −L H ÷ R.
Example of the last: a 500.000 m base at a mean height of 250 m, with R = 6370 km, needs −500 × 250 ÷ 6 370 000 = −0.020 m, giving 499.980 m.

Use of the base: with adjusted angles A = 62°18′05″, B = 57°42′00″, C = 59°59′55″, BC = 499.980 × 0.88540 ÷ 0.86601 = 511.17 m and AC = 499.980 × 0.84526 ÷ 0.86601 = 488.00 m. The coordinates of C computed from A and from B agree within 0.01 m.
Today the base is measured by EDM, and in trilateration every side is measured, with angles computed by the cosine rule; the sine-rule logic remains the check.

bank.q: Two stations P and Q are on a line towards a chimney whose base is inaccessible, Q being 40.000 m farther from it than P. A staff on a benchmark of RL 250.000 m reads 1.420 m from P and 1.865 m from Q with the telescope horizontal. The vertical angles to the top of the chimney are 15°20′ from P and 11°40′ from Q. Find the horizontal distance from P and the RL of the top. Take tan 15°20′ = 0.27419 and tan 11°40′ = 0.20648.
outline: Axis RLs at P and Q
D from the single plane formula
RL from P; check from Q
answer: Sketch: the chimney at the right; Q farthest, then P nearer, on one line; horizontal lines from each instrument axis; the two lines of sight meeting at the top T.
d = axis at Q − axis at P = 251.865 − 251.420 = +0.445 m (the axis at Q is higher).

Let D be the horizontal distance from P to the chimney. Height of T above the axis at P: h₁ = D tan α₁. Above the axis at Q: h₂ = (D + 40.000) tan α₂. Since RL of T is the same, 251.420 + h₁ = 251.865 + h₂, so h₁ − h₂ = d.
D tan α₁ − (D + s) tan α₂ = d gives D = (s tan α₂ + d) ÷ (tan α₁ − tan α₂).
Height of the chimney above the benchmark = 286.667 − 250.000 = 36.667 m.
Curvature and refraction: at 0.17 km the combined correction is 0.0673 × 0.17² = 0.002 m, negligible.

Note on the sign of d: had the axis at Q been lower, d would be negative and the numerator smaller; using d with the wrong sign here would give D = (8.2592 − 0.445) ÷ 0.06771 = 115.40 m and an RL 3.6 m too low, which the check from Q would expose.

Why two stations are needed: with the base inaccessible, one vertical angle gives only the ratio of height to distance. The second angle from a station a known distance s farther back adds the second equation that fixes D.

Precision of the result: the denominator tan α₁ − tan α₂ = 0.06771 is small, so an error of 20″ in α₁ (0.00010 in its tangent) changes D by about 0.15 %, roughly 0.2 m, and the RL by about 0.04 m. Both angles are therefore read on both faces and meaned.
Field order: set up at P, take the benchmark reading with the telescope horizontal, then the face-left and face-right vertical angles to the top; repeat at Q; tape PQ in both directions.
Answer: D = 128.55 m from P; RL of the top 286.667 m.

bank.q: A tacheometer with K = 100 and C = 0.30 m is set up at station A (RL 210.500 m), its horizontal axis 1.400 m above the peg. A staff held vertically at B gives hair readings of 0.945, 1.640 and 2.335 m with a vertical angle of −6°40′ (depression). Find the horizontal distance AB and the RL of B. Comment on the accuracy of the result. Take cos 6°40′ = 0.99324 and sin 6°40′ = 0.11609.
outline: Inclined sight formulas with the constants
Sign of V for a depression
RL of B from the instrument axis
answer: Staff intercept s = 2.335 − 0.945 = 1.390 m. Mid-hair check: (0.945 + 2.335) ÷ 2 = 1.640 m, equal to the middle reading, so the readings are consistent.
The staff is vertical and the sight inclined, so D = K s cos²θ + C cos θ and V = K s sin θ cos θ + C sin θ.
The angle is a depression, so the point on the staff cut by the middle hair is 16.06 m below the instrument axis.
RL of instrument axis = 210.500 + 1.400 = 211.900 m.
Had the cos²θ been left out, D = 139.0 + 0.30 = 139.30 m, 1.9 m (1.4 %) too long, which shows why the inclined formula is needed even at moderate slopes.

Accuracy: stadia distances are good to about 1 in 500 to 1 in 1000, so D is uncertain by some 0.15 to 0.3 m; the RL is good to a few centimetres, enough for contouring and detail but not for control. A reading error of 1 mm in each outer hair changes s by up to 2 mm and D by about 0.2 m.

Field order at each staff station: plumb the staff with its bubble, read the three hairs, then the vertical angle with the altitude bubble centred, and the horizontal angle from the reference line; book all five together.
Plan position of B: with the horizontal angle from the reference line, D = 137.43 m fixes B in plan as a polar point from A, so one pointing gives both the position and the RL needed for contouring.

Comparison with a horizontal sight: on level ground the same intercept would give D = 139.0 + 0.30 = 139.30 m and V = 0; the inclination shortens the horizontal distance and adds the large vertical component.
Answer: AB = 137.43 m (horizontal); RL of B = 194.20 m.

bank.q: A closed traverse ABC is run clockwise. Observed interior angles: B 48°11′00″, C 63°34′10″, A 68°15′05″. The bearing of AB is 72°15′00″ and A is at E 500.000 m, N 800.000 m. Lengths: AB 312.40 m, BC 324.06 m, CA 259.97 m. Adjust the angles, compute the bearings, latitudes and departures, the closing error and precision, and the coordinates of B and C by Bowditch's rule.

answer.text: Departures (l sin β) and latitudes (l cos β):

answer: Closing error e = √(0.010² + 0.050²) = 0.051 m. Relative precision = 896.43 ÷ 0.051 = 1 in 17 600, acceptable for site control.
Check: the adjusted departures sum to 297.527 − 132.162 − 165.365 = 0.000 and the latitudes to 95.255 − 295.868 + 200.613 = 0.000, and the last line returns exactly to A.

Why angles first: an angular error turns every following bearing, which would show up as a large, systematic linear misclosure; the Bowditch rule is meant only for the small random errors left after the angles close.

Interior angle rule used: for a loop traversed clockwise with the interior angles on the right of the direction of travel, the back bearing of the previous line minus the interior angle gives the forward bearing; anticlockwise loops add the angle instead. A sketch of the loop with north drawn shows which applies.

Accuracy check of the result: the adjusted coordinates give BC = √(132.162² + 295.868²) = 324.04 m, within 0.02 m of the measured 324.06 m, so the adjustment has moved no line by more than the expected taping error.
If the specification had been 1 in 20 000, the traverse (1 in 17 600) would fail and the lines would be remeasured rather than adjusted.
Answer: B (797.527, 895.255) m and C (665.365, 599.387) m; closing error 0.051 m, precision about 1 in 17 600.

bank.q: Two straights meeting at chainage 1820.40 m with a deflection angle of 32° are to be joined by a circular curve of 400 m radius. Calculate the elements of the curve and the data for setting it out by Rankine's method with pegs at every 30 m of chainage.
outline: T, l, long chord, E, M
answer: Length of curve l = π × 400 × 32 ÷ 180 = 223.40 m. Long chord = 2 × 400 × sin 16° = 220.51 m. Apex distance E = 400(sec 16° − 1) = 16.12 m. Mid-ordinate M = 400(1 − cos 16°) = 15.50 m.

Pegs at 30 m chainages: the first is at 1710 m, so the first sub-chord is 1710 − 1705.70 = 4.30 m. Full chords of 30 m then reach 1920 m (seven of them), and the last sub-chord is 1929.10 − 1920 = 9.10 m. Check: 4.30 + 7 × 30 + 9.10 = 223.40 m.
Check: the total deflection to T₂ equals Δ/2 = 16°00′00″.

Field procedure: locate T₁ and T₂ by measuring T back and forward from I. Set the theodolite at T₁, sight I with the circle at 0°00′00″. Set the first total deflection 0°18′28″ and measure 4.30 m from T₁ along the line of sight to fix peg 1. Set 2°27′23″ and swing a 30 m tape from peg 1 until its end meets the line of sight: that is peg 2. Continue to T₂.
Closing check in the field: the last line of sight at 16°00′00″ should pass through T₂ already fixed from I; a miss shows an error in the chords or in T₁.

Data for the field book: the deflection for each peg is set on the circle with the telescope on I at zero; the chord is taped from the previous peg, not from T₁, so each peg depends on the one before it and errors build up towards T₂.

Alternative check: with a total station at T₁, the coordinates of each peg can be computed from chord lengths T₁ to peg, 2R sin(total deflection), for example 2 × 400 × sin 2°27′23″ = 34.29 m to peg 2.
Answer: T = 114.70 m, l = 223.40 m, T₁ at 1705.70 m, T₂ at 1929.10 m, with the table above.

bank.q: At a station O, the angles AOB = α and BOC = β were measured with weights 2 and 3, and the whole angle AOC was measured with weight 1: α = 38°12′20″, β = 41°25′35″, AOC = 79°37′45″. Find the most probable values by forming the normal equations, and check by the rule of distributing in proportion to 1 ÷ w.
answer: The condition is α + β = AOC. Observed α + β = 79°37′55″, which exceeds the observed AOC by 10″, so the observations do not agree and must be adjusted.
Let the most probable values be α = 38°12′20″ + x and β = 41°25′35″ + y, with x and y in seconds. The adjusted AOC is α + β = 79°37′55″ + x + y.
Observation equations (value of each observation in terms of the unknowns): x = 0 (weight 2); y = 0 (weight 3); x + y = 79°37′45″ − 79°37′55″ = −10″ (weight 1).
Normal equation for x: multiply each equation by its weight and by its coefficient of x and add: 2(x) + 1(x + y) = 1(−10), so 3x + y = −10.
Normal equation for y: 3(y) + 1(x + y) = −10, so x + 4y = −10.
Solve: from the first, y = −10 − 3x; then x + 4(−10 − 3x) = −10, so −11x = 30 and x = −2.73″. Then y = −10 + 8.18 = −1.82″.
Residuals (adjusted − observed): α −2.73″, β −1.82″, AOC +5.45″. Σwv² = 2(2.73²) + 3(1.82²) + 1(5.45²) = 14.9 + 9.9 + 29.7 = 54.5 (seconds squared).

Check by the rule: the discrepancy of 10″ is shared in proportion to 1 ÷ w, that is 1/2, 1/3 and 1, sum 11/6. Shares: α 10 × (1/2) ÷ (11/6) = 2.73″, β 10 × (1/3) ÷ (11/6) = 1.82″, AOC 10 × 1 ÷ (11/6) = 5.45″. The parts α and β are made smaller and the whole made larger, the same answer as the normal equations.

Standard error of unit weight: n = 3 observations, u = 2 unknowns, so σ₀ = √(54.5 ÷ 1) = 7.4″, the standard error of an angle measured once; α, of weight 2 before adjustment, had about 7.4 ÷ √2 = 5.2″.

Interpretation: the two parts α and β were each measured more carefully than the whole angle, so they move less; the whole angle, of weight 1, takes the largest correction. Had all three weights been equal, each would have moved by 10 ÷ 3 = 3.33″.

Why least squares: any values with α + β = AOC satisfy the condition; least squares picks the set that changes the observations least, measured by Σwv², which is also the most probable set when errors are random.

bank.q: Classify the errors in theodolite angle measurement as instrumental, personal and natural. For each, explain its effect on the angle and how it is eliminated or reduced. Show with numbers why some errors grow on steep sights.
outline: Instrumental: collimation, trunnion axis, vertical axis, eccentricity, graduation, index
Personal: centring, levelling, bisection, parallax, reading, clamps
Effect of c sec h and i tan h with numbers
Which cancel by face change and which do not

head: Error
Effect
Remedy
rows: Collimation (line of sight not ⟂ horizontal axis) by c
Direction in error by c sec h, h the vertical angle
Horizontal axis not ⟂ vertical axis, by i
Direction in error by i tan h
Error grows with tan h and does not reverse with face
Careful levelling; recheck the plate bubble
Each vernier reads high or low
All vertical angles off by a constant
Mean of both faces, or correct by the index error

answer: Personal errors: centring error (most serious on short sights: a 5 mm centring error on a 50 m sight changes the direction by up to 5 ÷ 50 000 rad ≈ 21″), imperfect levelling, inaccurate bisection of a thick or tilted target, parallax, misreading the vernier or booking wrongly, and using the wrong tangent screw. Remedies: careful centring with an optical plummet, sighting the foot of the ranging rod or a fine target, removing parallax, reading both verniers and both faces, and following a fixed routine.

Natural errors: horizontal refraction where a line grazes hot ground or a wall; heat shimmer at midday; wind vibrating the instrument; uneven heating of the tripod; settlement of the tripod on soft ground. Remedies: keep lines well above the ground, observe early or late in the day, shade the instrument, use a firm set-up, and observe quickly. None of these reverses on changing face.

Effect on steep sights, collimation: for a collimation error c = 20″, a sight at h = 0° is in error by 20″, but at h = 30° by 20 × sec 30° = 23.1″, and at h = 60° by 40″. An angle between a flat sight and a 60° sight carries 40 − 20 = 20″ of error.
Effect on steep sights, horizontal axis: for i = 20″, a flat sight has no error (tan 0° = 0), a 30° sight 20 × 0.577 = 11.5″, and a 60° sight 34.6″. This is why the spire test uses a steep sight.

Vertical axis tilt of 20″ has the same order of effect as the horizontal axis error on steep sights, but it does not change sign on changing face, so the face mean keeps it in full. Only levelling up carefully removes it.

Analysis: errors that change sign with the face (collimation, horizontal axis, index) cancel in the face mean; errors that do not (vertical axis, refraction, centring) must be prevented at the set-up. Errors that vary round the circle (graduation, eccentricity) are averaged by reading two verniers and by repetition on different parts of the circle.

Assessing the result: the spread between faces and between sets, the closure of the horizon at a station, and finally the angular misclosure of a traverse or triangle show whether the remaining random error is within the specification.

Conclusion: observe on both faces, read both verniers, use several sets with different initial settings, level and centre with care, and keep sights clear of the ground; then only small random errors remain, and these are shared by adjustment.

bank.q: Compare triangulation, trilateration, traversing and GNSS as methods of horizontal control. Recommend, with reasons, a scheme for controlling a 20 km highway corridor through mixed open country and a town.
outline: What each method measures and how it is checked
Vertical control for the same corridor
answer: Triangulation: measures one base and all angles; sides by the sine rule. Strong in open, hilly country with long intervisible lines; needs towers where the ground is flat; scale depends on the base; checks come from triangle closures, a check base and redundant figures.

Trilateration: measures all sides by EDM; angles by the cosine rule. Strong in scale and fast with modern EDM; a single triangle has no internal check, so braced figures with extra lines are needed; still needs intervisibility.

Traversing: measures lines and the angles between consecutive lines; follows a corridor and works through towns where long lines are blocked. Its errors grow with the number of stations, so it must close on itself or on known points; checks are the angular closure, (2n − 4) × 90° for a loop, and the linear misclosure, compared as 1 in (Σl ÷ e).

GNSS: measures positions from satellites; stations need a clear sky, not a view of each other. Gives E, N and ellipsoidal height in one session; accuracy of a few millimetres to centimetres with static or network methods; weak under trees, in narrow streets and near tall buildings.

Recommendation for a 20 km corridor: a primary frame of GNSS stations in pairs every 2 to 3 km along the route, each pair intervisible so that it also gives a bearing; fixed in static sessions from national reference stations and adjusted by least squares.
Within the open stretches, densify with total-station traverses between GNSS pairs (link traverses that start and close on known coordinates and bearings), with legs of 150 to 300 m.

Through the town, where sky is blocked, run a total-station traverse along the street between GNSS pairs on either side of the town, closing to better than 1 in 20 000, and adjust by Bowditch's rule or least squares.

Triangulation in the classical sense would be slow over 20 km of flat country and needs towers; it is used only where a river or valley must be crossed, as a braced quadrilateral across the gap measured by both angles and distances.

Vertical control: carry levels by double-run differential levelling along the corridor between national benchmarks, with benchmarks every 250 to 500 m, accepting a closure of C√K mm; GNSS heights alone are not used for drainage gradients unless converted with a good geoid model and checked on benchmarks.
Conclusion: GNSS for the frame, traverses for density and for the town, levelling for heights; every part closed on something known.

bank.q: Justify the use of a transition curve between a straight and a circular curve. For a road curve of radius 450 m and deflection angle 36°, with a design speed of 90 km/h, find the length of transition by the rate of change of radial acceleration (0.5 m/s³) and by the rate of applying superelevation (maximum 0.07, carriageway 7.5 m, raised at 1 in 150). Adopt a length and find the shift and the total tangent length.
outline: Why: radial acceleration and cant applied gradually
Ideal spiral r l = R L<sub>s</sub>
Equilibrium e, the cap, and length by cant
answer: Need for a transition: on a straight the radius is infinite and the radial acceleration zero; on the circular arc it is V² ÷ R. Without a transition the full acceleration, and the superelevation that balances it, would appear at the tangent point at once, giving a jerk and making the outer edge of the road rise abruptly. A transition increases the curvature steadily, so the acceleration grows at a controlled rate and the superelevation can be run in over its length.

Other benefits: the vehicle follows the natural path of a driver turning the wheel steadily, the widening of the carriageway on the curve can be applied gradually, and the appearance of the road is smoother.
Ideal transition: the radius r at a distance l from the tangent satisfies r l = R L<sub>s</sub>, a clothoid; for setting out, the offsets are y = x³ ÷ (6 R L<sub>s</sub>) (the cubic parabola).
Length by the rate of change of radial acceleration: V = 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25.0 m/s. L<sub>s</sub> = V³ ÷ (c R) = 15 625 ÷ (0.5 × 450) = 69.4 m.

Equilibrium superelevation: e = V² ÷ (g R) = 625 ÷ (9.81 × 450) = 0.142. This exceeds the maximum of 0.07, so e = 0.07 is provided and the rest (0.142 − 0.07 = 0.072) is carried by side friction between tyre and road, which is well within what a dry road gives.
Length by superelevation: the outer edge rises by e × width = 0.07 × 7.5 = 0.525 m. At a rate of 1 in 150 this needs 0.525 × 150 = 78.8 m.
Adopt the larger value, rounded up: L<sub>s</sub> = 80 m.
Shift S = L<sub>s</sub>² ÷ (24 R) = 6400 ÷ 10 800 = 0.59 m. The circular arc is moved inward by this amount to make room for the transitions.
Total tangent length from I to the start of the transition = (R + S) tan(Δ/2) + L<sub>s</sub> ÷ 2 = (450 + 0.59) × tan 18° + 40 = 450.59 × 0.32492 + 40 = 146.41 + 40 = 186.41 m.

Check of the arc left between the transitions: each transition turns the direction through L<sub>s</sub> ÷ (2R) rad = 80 ÷ 900 = 0.0889 rad = 5.09°, so the two together take 10.19° of the 36°, leaving 25.81° for the circular arc, a length of 450 × 0.4505 = 202.7 m. The arc is long enough, so the design works.

Evaluation: governed here by superelevation, not by comfort; on a sharper curve or at a higher speed the comfort criterion would govern. A transition of 80 m costs little extra land and greatly improves safety at 90 km/h.
